title: Pulmonary Function Tests: Obstruction, Restriction, Diffusion, Then Context
bottomLine: Pulmonary function tests describe physiology; they do not diagnose disease by themselves. Confirm test quality, identify obstruction, confirm true restriction with lung volumes rather than low FVC alone, and use diffusion/bronchodilator response in clinical context.
recognize: A reduced expiratory ratio supports obstruction when the test is technically valid.
Low FVC can reflect restriction, air trapping, mixed disease or poor effort; restriction requires reduced total lung capacity.
Reduced diffusion can occur with emphysema, ILD, pulmonary vascular disease or anemia.
differentiate: Obstruction is not synonymous with COPD; asthma, bronchiectasis and other airway diseases can obstruct.
Absence of a large single bronchodilator response does not exclude asthma when the clinical pattern remains convincing.
assessment: Confirm quality/effort and review symptoms, smoking/exposures, inhaled therapy, prior testing, anemia context and clinical stability at testing.
workup: Interpret spirometry, lung volumes and diffusion together when available; use full PFTs or specialty testing when baseline spirometry cannot answer the clinical question.
management: Treat the clinical diagnosis supported by the physiology and rest of the assessment; refer unexplained restriction, markedly reduced diffusion or discordant patterns to respirology.
medicationSafety: Do not escalate chronic inhaled therapy solely because one poor-quality spirometry attempt looks obstructive.
redFlags: Restrictive physiology plus ILD/systemic red flags
counselling: Explain that PFTs describe how the lungs behave; history, examination, imaging and other tests identify why.
followUp: Repeat PFTs when the result will assess progression, treatment response or a defined diagnostic question.
examTrap: Calling a low FVC restrictive lung disease without confirming reduced total lung capacity.
oneLinePearl: Spirometry finds airflow patterns; lung volumes confirm restriction; diffusion helps explain gas-exchange disease.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society pulmonary-function practice resources

title: Oxygen Therapy: Treat Hypoxemia, Prescribe the Need, Reassess the Device
bottomLine: Oxygen is a drug/device therapy for hypoxemia or selected high-risk states, not a reflex treatment for breathlessness with normal oxygenation. Match the delivery system and target to the syndrome, reassess response, and use formal criteria for long-term home oxygen.
recognize: Acute oxygen need is driven by oxygenation and clinical status, not dyspnea intensity alone.
Chronic home oxygen requires documented disease-specific criteria and reassessment rather than continuation because the patient feels better with it.
differentiate: Normoxemic dyspnea needs the cause treated; routine oxygen does not replace bronchodilation, diuresis, anticoagulation or other disease-specific therapy.
Patients at risk for hypercapnic respiratory failure still require oxygen when hypoxemic, but titration and blood-gas reassessment matter.
assessment: Assess SpO2 reliability, work of breathing, mental status, perfusion, diagnosis, prior CO2 retention, current device/interface and response to therapy.
workup: Use blood-gas assessment when ventilation/CO2 failure or severe gas-exchange disturbance is a concern; formal home-oxygen qualification follows current Canadian/local criteria.
management: Titrate oxygen to the target appropriate for the clinical context while treating the underlying cause; escalate respiratory support when simple oxygen is inadequate and reassess need after stabilization.
medicationSafety: Excess oxygen can worsen hypercapnia in susceptible patients, but fear of CO2 retention must not justify untreated severe hypoxemia.
Home oxygen creates major fire risk; smoking/open-flame safety is mandatory.
redFlags: Need for noninvasive or invasive ventilatory support
counselling: Teach device use, prescribed flow/target, fire safety and when worsening symptoms require reassessment rather than simply increasing home oxygen.
followUp: Reassess chronic oxygen need after major clinical changes or recovery from an acute exacerbation according to the respiratory program.
examTrap: Giving oxygen as the primary treatment for normoxemic dyspnea—or withholding needed oxygen from severe COPD hypoxemia because of CO2-retention fear.
oneLinePearl: Oxygen treats hypoxemia; ventilation treats CO2 failure; both require treatment of the cause.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society oxygen/home respiratory care principles

title: Pulmonary Nodule: Estimate Cancer Risk Before Ordering the Next Scan
bottomLine: An incidental pulmonary nodule is managed by malignancy probability, size/morphology, growth, patient risk and whether the patient could benefit from treatment. Compare prior imaging first, then choose surveillance, PET/CT, biopsy or specialty referral rather than repeating CT indefinitely.
recognize: Risk rises with older age, smoking history, prior cancer, suspicious morphology, upper-lobe location and documented growth.
Many small nodules are benign and over-imaging can cause radiation, anxiety and invasive downstream harm.
differentiate: A nodule found during formal lung-cancer screening follows the screening program algorithm; an incidental nodule follows an incidental-nodule pathway.
Hemoptysis or weight loss shifts the patient toward diagnostic evaluation rather than routine surveillance.
assessment: Review exact size, density, morphology, number, prior imaging/growth, smoking exposure, age, prior malignancy and treatment preferences/fitness.
workup: Retrieve prior imaging before ordering another scan whenever possible and use a validated risk/pathway framework to determine surveillance, PET/CT, biopsy or referral.
management: Follow current Canadian/provincial lung-nodule and screening pathways; refer moderate/high-risk, growing or technically concerning nodules for respirology/thoracic/oncology assessment.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary contrast or invasive biopsy when surveillance is the evidence-based next step; consider renal, allergy and bleeding risk for downstream procedures.
counselling: Explain absolute cancer risk and why surveillance can be safer than immediate biopsy for low-risk nodules.
followUp: Create a closed-loop recall system so surveillance imaging is not lost and document completion or handoff of responsibility.
examTrap: Ordering yearly CT forever for a stable low-risk nodule—or biopsying a tiny low-risk lesion before reviewing prior imaging.
oneLinePearl: Pulmonary nodule care is risk-stratified surveillance, not reflex biopsy or endless scanning.
sourceBasis: Cancer Care Ontario lung cancer pathway maps

title: Interstitial Lung Disease: Recognize Restriction, Exposures, Autoimmune Clues, and Progression
bottomLine: Interstitial lung disease is a family of diffuse parenchymal disorders. Suspect it in persistent exertional dyspnea, dry cough, crackles, restriction or diffusion impairment; obtain exposure/medication/autoimmune history and appropriate HRCT/PFT assessment, then refer early because subtype and progression determine treatment.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, fine inspiratory crackles, clubbing, restrictive physiology and reduced diffusion capacity are common clues.
Connective-tissue disease, occupational/environmental exposures, medications, radiation and hypersensitivity exposures can drive ILD.
differentiate: Heart failure, COPD/emphysema, obesity, infection and pulmonary vascular disease can mimic or coexist with ILD.
Acute ILD exacerbation is different from gradual chronic progression and requires hospital-level evaluation.
assessment: Take detailed occupational, home/bird/mould, medication, smoking/vaping and autoimmune histories and assess oxygenation, function, crackles, clubbing and systemic rheumatologic features.
workup: Use high-resolution CT and complete PFTs including diffusion capacity; order targeted autoimmune/exposure testing by phenotype and consider multidisciplinary specialist classification.
Before significant immunosuppression, use current CTS infection-screening guidance.
management: Remove harmful exposures when identified, provide vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation/oxygen assessment and comorbidity care, and coordinate subtype-specific antifibrotic or immunosuppressive therapy through respirology.
medicationSafety: Do not empirically start chronic systemic corticosteroids for undifferentiated fibrotic ILD; some subtypes are not steroid-responsive and immunosuppression can be harmful.
Screen infection risk before significant immunosuppression.
counselling: Explain that ILD is a group of diseases and treatment depends on the exact subtype and trajectory.
followUp: Trend symptoms, oxygenation, PFTs and imaging through specialist care and address transplant/palliative planning when disease advances.
examTrap: Escalating inhalers or empiric steroids indefinitely for progressive restriction and crackles without HRCT/subtype evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Dry cough plus crackles plus restriction should trigger an interstitial-disease workup, not another bronchodilator refill.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society ILD resources and 2026 infection-screening position statement

title: Occupational Lung Disease: The Work History Is Part of the Diagnostic Test
bottomLine: Occupational lung disease is missed when the clinician asks only what job the patient has. Define tasks, agents, timing, protective controls and whether symptoms improve away from work; then use objective testing and exposure control before simply escalating medications.
recognize: Work-related asthma, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, pneumoconiosis and irritant injury can present with cough, wheeze, dyspnea or restrictive disease.
Symptoms that improve on weekends or vacations are a high-yield clue for work-related asthma but absence of that pattern does not exclude chronic occupational disease.
differentiate: New sensitizer-induced occupational asthma differs from work-exacerbated pre-existing asthma, while fibrotic exposure diseases may persist away from work.
A normal chest x-ray does not exclude early occupational asthma or all occupational ILD.
assessment: Ask employer/industry, specific tasks, dusts/fumes/vapours/biologic agents, PPE/ventilation, co-worker illness, latency, acute high-level events and symptom timing on/off work.
workup: Use spirometry and serial objective measurements across work/off-work periods when asthma is suspected; use HRCT/PFT/exposure-specific evaluation when occupational ILD is plausible.
management: Reduce or remove harmful exposure when feasible, optimize disease-specific treatment and involve occupational medicine/respirology early when ongoing exposure risks permanent loss of function.
medicationSafety: Escalating medication while leaving a sensitizing exposure unchanged is incomplete treatment.
Do not misrepresent the archived 1998 CTS occupational-asthma guideline as current operational law; local workplace/compensation requirements vary.
redFlags: Inability to avoid a high-risk exposure
counselling: Discuss workplace accommodation and reporting/compensation pathways without guaranteeing legal eligibility or outcome.
followUp: Document objective findings and exposure timing carefully and close the loop on specialist/occupational referrals.
examTrap: Treating repeated work-week respiratory flares without asking which specific exposure occurs during the shift.
oneLinePearl: In occupational lung disease, timing and task can be as diagnostic as the spirometry.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society current guideline-status library and occupational respiratory practice

title: Lung Cancer Screening: Screening Is for High-Risk Asymptomatic Patients
bottomLine: Lung-cancer screening and diagnostic evaluation are different pathways. Use the current provincial or territorial program for eligible asymptomatic high-risk patients; hemoptysis, unexplained weight loss, persistent focal symptoms or a suspicious nodule requires diagnostic workup instead of a screening interval.
recognize: Screening eligibility is defined by the current jurisdictional program and can change as implementation evolves.
A screening LDCT result requires structured follow-up; the scan itself is not the endpoint.
differentiate: New symptoms move the patient from screening to diagnostic assessment.
Chest radiography is not an equivalent substitute for LDCT within an organized screening program.
assessment: Clarify symptoms first, then smoking history, age, prior cancer/nodule history, ability to complete downstream diagnostic/treatment evaluation and local program access.
workup: Use current LDCT screening pathways for eligible asymptomatic patients and diagnostic CT/other testing for symptoms or suspicious findings.
management: Refer eligible patients to the organized screening program, assign ownership of abnormal follow-up and provide smoking-cessation support regardless of screening eligibility.
medicationSafety: Avoid repeated empiric antibiotics or steroids that delay diagnostic assessment of persistent suspicious respiratory symptoms.
counselling: Explain screening benefits, false positives, incidental findings and the need for follow-up if the CT is abnormal.
followUp: Track the exact next imaging or diagnostic step until the finding is resolved or entered into a defined surveillance plan.
examTrap: Ordering routine screening LDCT for a patient with hemoptysis instead of starting a diagnostic pathway.
oneLinePearl: No symptoms means screening; symptoms mean diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Cancer Care Ontario lung screening/pathway resources

title: Acute Bronchitis vs Pneumonia: Decide Who Needs Imaging and Antibiotics
bottomLine: Most acute bronchitis is viral and does not benefit from antibiotics. Identify pneumonia or another serious cause using vital signs, oxygenation, focal examination findings, host risk and imaging when indicated—not sputum colour or cough duration alone.
recognize: Bronchitis often causes cough with or without sputum after a viral syndrome while the patient remains systemically stable.
Pneumonia becomes more likely with abnormal vital signs, hypoxemia, focal lung findings, pleuritic pain or a high-risk host.
differentiate: Green or yellow sputum does not prove bacterial infection.
Pertussis, asthma/COPD exacerbation, PE, heart failure, influenza and COVID can present with cough and require different pathways.
assessment: Assess respiratory rate, heart rate, temperature, oxygen saturation, work of breathing, focal chest findings, pregnancy, age/frailty, immunocompromise and duration/exposure history.
workup: Avoid routine chest radiography for a low-risk patient with normal vital signs/examination when pneumonia is unlikely; obtain imaging when pneumonia is clinically plausible or the course is atypical/high risk.
Use viral or pertussis testing when the result will change treatment, infection control or public-health action.
management: Provide supportive symptom care for uncomplicated bronchitis and avoid routine antibiotics.
Treat clinically supported pneumonia using current Canadian/local guidance and escalate instability or significant hypoxemia.
medicationSafety: Antibiotics expose patients to allergy, C. difficile, interactions and resistance without benefit in uncomplicated viral bronchitis.
Avoid routine sedating/opioid cough suppressants in higher-risk patients without a clear indication.
redFlags: Failure to improve or new hemoptysis
counselling: Explain the expected cough course and give specific return precautions so 'no antibiotic today' is paired with an active care plan.
followUp: Reassess if fever, dyspnea, pleuritic pain, hypoxemia or prolonged/worsening symptoms develop.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics because sputum is coloured despite normal vital signs, normal oxygenation and no focal pneumonia findings.
oneLinePearl: Bronchitis is a cough syndrome; pneumonia is a lung infection with clinical evidence that justifies imaging and/or antibiotics.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Cold Standard respiratory stewardship
